title: Is the Economy Booming, or Just Growing?

scenes.purpose: Set the two facts side by side that seem to contradict each other.

visual.description: Split field: "The economy grew" lands on the left in green as the first clause is spoken; "The paycheck bought less" lands on the right in red on "bought less".

scenes.direction: Cold open; the second line punches in on "bought less".
scenes.narration: The American economy grew in both quarters of 2026 we have numbers for, and yet by September the average hourly paycheck bought less than it had a year before.

scenes.purpose: Pose the question the video answers.

visual.description: The question types on word by word, large and centred; "boom" and "backwards" take the two colours from the previous scene.

scenes.direction: Hold on the question through s03.
scenes.narration: So is this a boom, or are workers going backwards? Which side is right depends on which number you look at.

scenes.purpose: Give the boom side in its own words.

visual.description: Quote card, text only: the line sets in large serif; "by far" holds and turns amber.
onScreenText: "The economy is the greatest economy we've ever had by far."

scenes.direction: Hard cut in; hold half a second after the quote.
scenes.narration: Donald Trump has put one side plainly: "The economy is the greatest economy we've ever had by far."

scenes.purpose: Give the paycheck side in its own words.

visual.description: Quote card, text only, mirrored from the previous one; "eating up" turns red as it is spoken.
onScreenText: "is really just eating up all of the wage growth"

scenes.direction: Wipe from the previous quote card.
scenes.narration: The other side points at the paycheck, and CBS News put it bluntly: inflation "is really just eating up all of the wage growth that Trump has talked about and then some".

scenes.purpose: Show the growth figures for the two quarters on record.

visual.description: Two horizontal bars, Q1 then Q2 2026, growing in as each figure is spoken; values printed at the bar ends.

chart.title: Real GDP growth, annual rate
chart.note: Annualised quarterly rates; the third quarter is not yet published.

scenes.direction: Question line first, then the bars build on "2.5" and "2.2".
scenes.narration: Start with the boom: how fast is the economy actually growing? Real GDP, the value of everything the country produces after stripping out price rises, grew at an annual rate of 2.5 percent in the first quarter of 2026 and 2.2 percent in the second.

scenes.purpose: Put the growth against the Fed's long-run pace so the viewer sees it is only a little above normal.

visual.description: The two quarter bars stay; a third bar for the Fed's long-run pace grows in below them, nearly as long. The small gap between them is the point.

chart.title: Growth against the long-run pace
chart.note: The long-run figure is the median FOMC projection, not a measurement.

scenes.direction: The long-run bar lands on "2.0 percent"; hold a beat on "not the surge".
scenes.narration: That is solid growth, but Federal Reserve officials put the economy's long-run pace at 2.0 percent a year, so this runs only a little above normal, not the surge the word boom suggests.

scenes.purpose: Show unemployment is low and steady.

visual.description: Three tiles: September's rate large in the centre, the low and high since March smaller either side.

scenes.direction: The centre tile lands on "4.2 percent", the side tiles on "4.1 and 4.3".
scenes.narration: What about jobs? The unemployment rate was 4.2 percent in September, and it has stayed between 4.1 and 4.3 percent since March.

scenes.purpose: Give the Fed chair's reading of that rate.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "full employment" turns amber as it is spoken.
onScreenText: "the unemployment rate is basically running consistent with full employment"

citations.label: Federal Reserve chair, press conference, 16 September 2026

scenes.narration: At its September press conference, the Federal Reserve's chair said "the unemployment rate is basically running consistent with full employment".

scenes.purpose: Show how little hiring there was.

visual.description: One tile, small for a jobs number: +29,000 counts up and stops short.

scenes.narration: But payrolls barely moved: employers added just 29,000 jobs in September.

scenes.purpose: Mark full employment as a judgement, not a measured fact.

visual.description: Large title, "judgement" in amber; "measurement" struck through lightly.

scenes.narration: And the jobs report itself never defines full employment, so calling this full employment is a judgement, not a measurement.

scenes.purpose: Start the paycheck with the year when pay beat prices.

visual.description: One green tile: real hourly earnings up 1.2 percent in the year to January 2026.

chart.title: Real hourly earnings, year to January 2026
chart.note: Average hourly earnings of all private employees, deflated by CPI.

citations.label: BLS, real average hourly earnings, January 2026

scenes.narration: Now the paycheck, the number most people actually feel. In the year to January 2026, pay beat prices, and average hourly earnings after inflation were up 1.2 percent.

scenes.purpose: Show real pay dropping below a year earlier from April on.

visual.description: Monthly column chart drawn as a diagram, March to September 2026, year-on-year change in real average hourly earnings, a zero line across the middle. Columns in order with labels: Mar +0.1, Apr -0.2, May -0.8, Jun -0.1, Jul -0.1, Aug -0.2, Sep -0.7. March is a thin green column just above zero; from April each column drops below the line in red, one by one, as "from April on" is spoken. Axis label: "Real hourly pay vs a year earlier, %". No other text.
onScreenText: Real hourly pay vs a year earlier

citations.label: BLS, real average hourly earnings, March to September 2026

scenes.direction: Columns drop in left to right, the April column on "April".
scenes.narration: Then prices jumped in the spring, and from April on, real hourly pay was lower than a year earlier in every month.

scenes.purpose: Show the September arithmetic: pay up 3.0, prices up 3.7, real pay down.

visual.description: Three tiles in a row: pay 3.0 percent, prices 3.7 percent, then real hourly earnings 0.7 percent lower in red, each landing as it is spoken.

chart.title: September 2026, change on a year earlier

scenes.direction: Tiles land on "3.0", "3.7" and "0.7"; the last one punches in.
scenes.narration: By September, pay was up 3.0 percent on the year and prices 3.7 percent, leaving real hourly earnings 0.7 percent lower.

scenes.purpose: Test the claim that wages beat inflation against the two dates.

visual.description: Quote card, text only: the quoted words set large; it holds through the sentence.

citations.label: BLS, real average hourly earnings, January 2026

scenes.narration: Trump's boast that wages are "rising much faster than inflation" matched the year to January; it does not match the year to September.

scenes.purpose: State the limit of the earnings figures.

visual.description: Small title on a quiet field: "Averages across all employees".

scenes.narration: One limit: these are averages across all employees, so they cannot tell you how the worker in the middle of the pay scale did.

scenes.purpose: Give the answer with the numbers it rests on.

visual.description: Four tiles land in order as the answer names each measure: growth, the long-run pace, unemployment, jobs added.

scenes.direction: Beat after "no"; tiles land on "growing", "long-run pace", "unemployment", "slow hiring".
scenes.narration: So is the economy booming? By these measures, no: it is growing a little faster than the Fed's long-run pace, with unemployment right at the level Fed officials expect it to settle at, but slow hiring.

scenes.purpose: Resolve the apparent contradiction: different measurements.

visual.description: Three short lines build one after another as each measure is named.

scenes.direction: Each line lands as it is spoken.
scenes.narration: Growth and shrinking real pay are not a contradiction: in 2026 they ran side by side, because output, jobs and what a paycheck buys are different measurements.

scenes.purpose: Leave the viewer with the one question to ask.

visual.description: The question types on large and centred, then holds.

scenes.direction: Types on with the last words; hold 2 s to end.
scenes.narration: So the next time someone tells you the economy is booming, or that it is broken, ask one question: which number?
